Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT A. Francisco Gold Condominium II Bldg, EDSA corner Mapagmahal St., Diliman, Quezon City OFFICE OF THE UNDERSECRETARY FOR LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG OPINION NO. 1.3 S. 2010 09 February 2010 GOVERNOR JESUS N. SACDALAN VICE-GOVERNOR EMMANUEL F. PINOL Provincial Capitol Building Province of Cotabato Géntlemen: This has reference to your earlier separate letters, which we herein consolidated, considering that they both pertain to one subject matter. Per your letters, the Sangguniang Panlalawigan held its regular session on 12 January 2010 where that August Body embarked upon the approval of the Annual Budget. According to you, all fourteen (14) members of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan attended said session, namely: ten (10) regular Sangguniang Pan/a/awigan Members, thræ (3) ex-omcio Sangguniang Pan/a/awigan Members and the Vice-Govemor as the Presiding Omcer. You further represented that when said approval of the Annual Budget was submitted for votation of said August Body, the result was: seven (7) members voted for the approva/ of the Annual Budget and six (6) voted against. Specifically, you want us to shed light on the following issues: "I) Whether or not the august body has reached the required of all the members of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan as provided for in Sections 53 and 54 of the Local Government Code and in relation to Article 107 (g) of its implementing Rules and Regulations? 2) Whether or not the vice governor as the presiding omcer is included in the count in determining the of all the members of the sangguniang panlalawigan to validly pass an appropriation ordinance? 3) Whether or not the board member who signed the Committee Report endorsing the 2010 Proposed Annual Performance Budget may withdraw without just and valid cause his thereon and vote against the approval thereof? 4) In the event that the Province operates under a re-enacted budget, what are those expenditures include< in the term "essential operating expenses" that may be incurred by the Province?"

We shall answer your first, second and third queries in one (1) discussion considering that they are interrelated. A reading of Governor Sacdalan's letter would give us an impression that he holds the view that a qualified majority is required to validly pass an Appropriation Ordinance. In a follow-up made to this Department by the Provincial Legal Officer of that Province, it was represented that the basis for this view is Article 107, 2nd sentence of paragraph (g) of the Implementing Rules and Regulations of the Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160), which provides that Any ordinance or resolution authorizing or directing the payment of money or creating liability, shall require the amrmative vote of a majority of au the sanggunian members for its passage" Hence, With this representation, it appears that they consider the Appropriation Ordinance as an ordinance authorizing or directing the payment of money so that it requires the vote of a majority of all the Sangguniang Panlalawigan Members for its On the other hand, as could be gleaned from Vice-Governor Piöol's letter, he is of the view that a two-thirds (2/3) vote is necessary to pass an Appropriation Ordinance. In fact, he himself declared in the said regular session that a 2/3 vote is necessary to pass the Appropriation Ordinance. Considering that there were only seven (7) members of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan who voted for the approval of the Appropriation Ordinance, Vice-governor Piöol also dedared in that session that the Appropriation Ordinance was not approved. It was also mentioned in this letter of Vice-Governor Piöol that still another camp, Sangguniang Panlalawigan Member Celestino Rapacon, fre Chairman of the Committee on Laws and Rules, holds another view that since the Local Govemment Code of 1991 (RA 7160) and that August Body's Internal Rules of Procedure (IRP) do not clearly specify that a 2/3 vote is needed to approve budget, it is understood that only a simple majority which is a vote Of seven (7) in favor and six (6) against is needed to approve the same. For purposes of clarity, please allow us to discuss the terms quorum, "simple majority," and "qualified majority." For the sanggunian to officially transact business, there should be a quorum. A quorum is defined by Section 53 of the Local Government Code of 1991 as referring to the presence of the majority of all the members of tie sanggunian who have been duly elected and qualified. Relative thereto, generally, ordinary measures require for its enactment only the approval of a simple majority of the sanggunian members present, there being a quorum. These perbin to tie normal transactions of the sanggunian which are approved by the sanggunian through a vote of simple majority of those present. On other hand, there are certain measures where the Local Government Code requires for its approval the vote of majority of all the members who were duly elected and qualified. -mis is what we call approval by the qualified majority of the sanggunian. In this case, the approval is to be voted not just by the majority of those present in a session there being a quorum but by the majority of all the members of the sanggunian duly elected and qualified regardless of whether ail of them were present or not in a particular session, there being a quorum.

Having these definitions in mind, may we now invite your attention to the following provisions of the Local Government Code of 1991, viz: "SECTION 319. Legislative Authorization of the - On or before the end of the current fiscal year, the sangunian concerned shall enact, through an ordinance, the annual of the local govemment unit for the ensuing fiscal year on the basis of the estimates of income and expenditures submitted by the local chief executive." "SECTION 468. Powrs, Duties, Functions and C.ensation. (a) The sangguniang as the legislative body of the province, shall enact ordinances, approve resolutions and appropriate funds for the general of the province and its inhabitants pursuant to Section 16 of this Code and in the proper exercise of the corporate powers of the province as provided for under Section 22 of this Code, and shall: (2) Generate and ma*mize the use of resources and revenues for the development plans, progam objectives and priorities of the province as provided for under Section 18 of this Code, with particular attention to ago-industrial development and country-wide growth and progress and relative thereto, shall: (i) Enact the annual and supplemental appropriations of the provincial government and appropriate for specific progams, projects, services and activities of the province, or for other purposes not contrary to law, in order to promote the general welfare of the province and its inhabitants;" Based on the foregoing, on or before the end of the current fiscal year, the sanggunian concerned (the Sangguniang Panlalawigan in your case) shah enæt, through an ordinance, the annual budget of the Province of Cobbato for the ensuing fiscal year on the basis of the estimates of income and expenditures submitted by Governor Sacdalan. The legislative instrument authorizing the budget is known as an Appropriation Ordinance. Please note that Sedion 468 (2)(i) of the Local Government Code of 1991, providing for the powers of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan vesG unto said enggunian tie power to appropriate the annual and supplemental appropriations of the provincial government, and appropriate funds for specific programs, projects, services and activities of the province, and for other purposes not contrary to law. It is to be noted that with respect to the enactment of the annual and supplemental appropriations, the law is silent as to what kind of majority vote is required of that sanggunian, unlike succeeding provisions which specifically require qualified majority vote of that sanggunian their passage. In iG silence, presumpüon is, tte same is be enacted only by a simple majority vote.

-4- As to the argument that the Appropriation is an ordinance authorizing or •directing the payment of money so that it requires the vote of a majority of aii Sangguniang Panlalawigan Members for iG passage, Sedion 55 of the Local Government Code of 1991 would bolster the position that the Appropriation Ordinance and an Ordinance directing the payment of money or creating liability are different when said provision treated them separately. Section 55 (b) of the same Code provides that: "The local chief executive, except the punong barangay, shall have the power to veto any particular item or items of an appropriations ordinance, an ordinance or resolution adopting a local development plan and public investment progam, or an or&ance directing the payment of money or creating liability m". As already mentioned, the Appropriation Ordinance is the legislative instrument authorizing the annual budget. Hence, what is there to be authorized by the sanggunian is the Annual Budget. An Annual Budget does not provide for the direction to pay or create a liability but it refers to a financial plan embodying the of income and expendiWres for one (1) fisal year operation of a local government unit. We are of the opinion that what is being referred to under Article 107, 2M sentence of paragraph (g) of the Implementing Rules and Regulations of the Local Government Code of 1991 which requires the approval of a qualified majority vote is an ordinance or resolution (specific appropriations) authorizing or direcbng the payment of money or creating a liability. Having determined the vote required in the enactment of the Appropriation Ordinance, which is simple majority, allow us to illustrate the compubtion of a simple rnajority based on the facts you represented in your leter. According to you, all fourteen (14) members of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan were present in the subjed regular session, namely: ten (10) regular .%ngguniang Pan/a/awigan thræ (3) ex-omcio .%ngguniang Panla/awigan and the Vice-Governor as the PresØing In determining a quorum, Section 53 of the Local Government Code of 1991 provides that a majority of all the members of the sanggunian who have elected and qualified shall constitute a quorum. Along this line, it bears to emphasize that per Section 467 (a) of the Local Government Code of 1991, the Sangguniang Panialawigan is a composite body where the Vice-Govemor as Presiding Officer is a composite member thereof. As a composite member in tie sangguniang panialawigan, he is therefore included in the determination of a quorum. "Majority" has been defined by the Supreme Court in Santiago vs. Guingona, et al (G.R. No. 134577, 18 November 1998) as Ü•.at which is greater half of the membership of the body or that number which is 50% + 1 of the entire membership. We note, however, that using either formula will us the same result. To illustrate, using the 50% + 1 forrnuia, tie 50% of a sanggunian composed of 14 members is 7. Hence, 7+1 will give us a sum of 8. On the other hand, if we use the second formula which is that number greater than half, then 8, in relation to 7, is definitely greater than the latter. The simple

majority of the sangguniang panlalawigan with fourteen (14) members where all of them were present in that particular session is therefore 8. Let it be noted that, in the instant case, the actual result of the votation as to the approval of the budget is 7-in favor and 6-against so that the 7 votes in favore obviously, feli one (i) vote short to satisfy the simple majority, which is eight (8). However, it has been represented by your Provincial Legal Officer that your Intemal Rules of Procedure provides under Section 15 thereof, that: "SECTION 15. DISSENTING VOTE. A committee member, unless he/she has entered his/her owections to the committee report or, in lieu thereof, has med with the Secretary to the Sangguniang &senting vote in writing before the report is submitted to the Body in open session, shan be presumed to have concurred with the report and shall thus be precluded from opposing it in the According to said Provincial Legal Officer, one (1) of the six (6) Sangguniang Panlalawigan Members who voted against the approval of the Appropriation Ordinance Budget is a member of the committee which favorably endorsed the same. It was not mentioned that said Sangguniang Panlalawigan Member has entered his objedion to the committee report recommending approvai of the annual budget nor has fiied with the Secretary to the Sangguniang Panlalawigan his dissenting vote in writing before the report is submitted to the August Body in open session. Hence, it was argued by the Provincial Legal Officer that, applying the aforequoted rule in your IRP, the said Sangguniang Panlalawigan Merr&r should be presumed to have concurred for the approval of your Appropriation Ordinance. We concur with this view of your Provinciai Legai Officer that the Sangguniang Panlalawigan Member who is a member of the committee, which favorably endorsed the Annual Budget, is precluded from voting against the approval of the Annual Appropriation Ordinance on the floor. Hence, nobvithstanding the fact that this Sangguniang Panlaiawigan Member voted against the passage of your Annual Appropriation Ordinance on the floor, his vote should be counted in addition to the seen (7) positive who voted in favor Of the approval of your Annuai Appropriation Ordinance to give into effect Secöon 15 of your IRP. Thus, in sum, there were eight (8) votes in favor of the approval of your Annual Appropriation Ordinance. Foregoing considered, we are of the view that your Annual Appropriation Ordinance was duly approved, finally, with respect to your fourth query, please be informed that there are two classes of expenditures namely, Current Operating Expenditures and Capital Outlay. Current Operating Expenditures are of two kinds namely, Personal Services and Maintenance Operating and Other Expenses (MOOE). Pursuant to the old Government Accounting and Auditing Manual and COA Circular No. 2002-005, the New Govemment Accounting and Auditing Manual,

MOOE includes expenses necessary for the regular operations of an agency. It particularly includes expenses for local or foreign travel, communication serv— repair and maintenance of govemment fadlibes, use, repairs and rnaintenarEe of govemment vehicles, transportation services, supplies and materialsr rent* interese, awards and indemnities, loan repayments and sinking fund contibutions, lossæ, depreciation, depletion, water, iiiumination and power service social security benefits, rewards and other claims, auditing services, training and seminars, extraordinary and miscellaneous expenses, confidential and intelligence expenses, anti-insurgency, contingency, emergency expenses, bxes and other duties, trading/production, advertising and publication expa•sæ, fidelity bond and insurance premiums, loss on foreign exchange, commitrnent fees, and other charges. As could be gleaned from the enumeration, we could logically conclude mat there are items in the MOOE which, t)ough may be necessary for me regular operation of the local government unit, but may not at all necessary far its basic operation. Accordingly, the expenses referred to by the phrase "essential operating expenses" could refer to some items in the MOOE which are essential for the conunued basic operation and existence of a local government unit. While essential operating expenses does not cover all of tie above enumerated MOOE items, however; should there be still available funds after the essential operating expenses are satisfied, a local government unit may include other items in the MOOE of the previous fiscal year's budget as deemed re- We hope that we have addressed your concern accordingly.
